title: Bag of Tricks for Efficient Text Classification
summary: The paper asks how far a very simple linear text classifier (bag of words/n-grams, low-rank factorization, fast loss) can go against deep neural networks while being orders of magnitude cheaper to train and evaluate. The proposed fastText model embeds and averages word and n-gram features into a hidden vector that is fed to a linear classifier trained with SGD and a linearly decaying learning rate, optionally with a Huffman-tree hierarchical softmax for large label spaces. Across eight sentiment datasets it matches char-CNN/char-CRNN and is close to VDCNN while training in seconds per epoch on CPU, and on the 312K-class YFCC100M tag-prediction task it reaches 46.1 prec@1 with bigrams versus 35.6 for Tagspace.

match_target.why: AG News with h = 10 and bigrams is the user-specified target and is the cheapest reproduction of the paper's central claim: a small 4-class dataset that Table 2 says trains in ~1 s per epoch on CPU with 20 threads, yet it exhibits the paper's headline effect (linear bag-of-ngrams model matching deep nets after adding bigrams).

tolerance.why: Rule 2: the paper reports no std/CI for Table 1, and the value is an accuracy-like percentage on the Zhang et al. (2015) AG News test split of 7,600 examples (>= 2,000), so the band is 1.0 absolute point on the % scale.

requirements.stmt: The classifier must be the rank-constrained linear model of Figure 1: a word/n-gram lookup matrix A whose rows are averaged into the text representation, followed by a linear classifier B.
requirements.quote: The word representations are then averaged into a text representation, which is in turn fed to a linear classifier.

requirements.stmt: The training objective is the negative log-likelihood over the softmax distribution of the class given the averaged feature vector.
requirements.quote: We use the softmax function f to compute the probability distribution over the predefined classes.

requirements.stmt: Optimization must be asynchronous SGD over multiple CPU threads with a linearly decaying learning rate (not Adam, not batch gradient descent).
requirements.quote: This model is trained asynchronously on multiple CPUs using stochastic gradient descent and a linearly decaying learning rate.

requirements.stmt: A hierarchical softmax built on a Huffman coding tree must be available for large output spaces, dropping training cost from O(kh) to O(h log2 k).
requirements.quote: we use a hierarchical softmax (Goodman, 2001) based on the Huffman coding tree (Mikolov et al., 2013).

requirements.stmt: Bigram/n-gram features must be added on top of bag of words to capture local word order; the bigram run is the target configuration.
requirements.quote: Instead, we use a bag of n-grams as additional features to capture some partial information about the local word order.

requirements.stmt: N-gram features must be mapped with the hashing trick (Mikolov et al. 2011 hash) into 10M bins when only bigrams are used and 100M bins otherwise.
requirements.quote: We maintain a fast and memory efficient mapping of the n-grams by using the hashing trick

requirements.stmt: The sentiment experiments must use 10 hidden units, 5 epochs, and a learning rate chosen on a validation set from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}.
requirements.quote: run fastText for 5 epochs with a learning rate selected on a validation set from {0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5}

requirements.stmt: The exact same hyper-parameters must be used for all eight sentiment datasets (no per-dataset tuning of h, epochs or n-gram order in the main table).
requirements.quote: FastText has been run with the same parameters for all the datasets.

requirements.stmt: Input to the classifier must be the normalized bag of features of the document (feature counts divided/averaged by the document representation), with A and B as the only weight matrices.
No pre-trained word embeddings may be used; all embeddings are learned jointly with the classifier.
requirements.quote: Unlike Tang et al. (2015), fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings

requirements.stmt: For the YFCC100M tag-prediction task, words and tags occurring fewer than 100 times must be removed and the train/validation/test split used as described (91,188,648 / 930,497 / 543,424 examples), with precision at 1 as the metric.
requirements.quote: We remove the words and tags occurring less than 100 times and split the data into a train, validation and test set.

requirements.stmt: Training must be run on CPU with 20 threads (the setting under which all reported training times were measured).
requirements.quote: while our models are trained on a CPU using 20 threads

data.name: AG News, Sogou News, DBPedia, Yelp P., Yelp F., Yahoo Answers, Amazon F., Amazon P. (Zhang et al., 2015 sentiment suite)
data.how_to_get: Public release accompanying Zhang, Zhao & LeCun (2015), 'Character-level Convolutional Networks for Text Classification' (arXiv:1502.01710); the widely used download mirror cited by that repo is https://goo.gl/JyCnZq. The paper states only: 'We employ the same 8 datasets and evaluation protocol of Zhang et al. (2015).'

data.name: YFCC100M (titles, captions, tags only - images unused)
data.how_to_get: YFCC100M multimedia collection (Thomee et al., 2016). The paper gives no URL and only promises a preprocessing script: 'We will release a script that recreates this dataset so that our numbers could be reproduced.' Recreate the splits by removing words and tags with fewer than 100 occurrences, yielding the reported 91,188,648 train / 930,497 validation / 543,424 test examples, 297,141 words and 312,116 tags.

stated_compute: Both char-CNN and VDCNN are trained on a NVIDIA Tesla K40 GPU, while our models are trained on a CPU using 20 threads.
